question: A station-class disconnecting switch, with no interrupter or arcing attachment, is to be opened. C37.30.1 says to first:
choices: Open it slowly to stretch the arc
Open it under load, since the blades can break full current
Close the grounding switch first
Make sure the switch is not carrying load, because disconnecting switches have no interrupting rating
explanation: Disconnecting, grounding, and horn-gap switches are not given interrupting ratings. Only small currents can be broken, following the annex guidance, and even those make an open arc. Confirm no load first, then operate the switch briskly.

question: After operating a gang-operated air switch, C37.30.1 says you should:
choices: Trust the handle position indicator
Check only the center phase
Measure voltage on the source side only
Look at each blade to confirm it is fully closed and latched, or fully open
explanation: Linkage can bend or slip, so one phase can hang partway. The guide wants a visual check of every blade after operation, and a check that each phase actually interrupted when the switch was opened.

question: While a switch is opening, the arc has not gone out by the time the blade is about two-thirds of the way open. C37.30.1 says to:
choices: Keep opening as fast as possible
Reclose the switch if practical
Stop the blade where it is and wait
Close the grounding switch
explanation: If the current has not interrupted by roughly two-thirds of travel, conditions are likely too severe for that switch. Reclosing, where practical, limits equipment damage and danger to people. Then use a device that is rated to interrupt.

question: Maintaining a de-energized air switch, you find light pitting on the contacts. C37.30.1 suggests:
choices: Filing the contacts flat with a coarse file
Smoothing it with clean, fine sandpaper, not emery, or as the manufacturer recommends, with grounds on both sides of the switch
Grinding with an emery wheel
Leaving it, since pitting does not affect contact resistance
explanation: Minor pitting can be dressed with clean, fine sandpaper, and the guide says specifically not to use emery. Before any work, the switch is disconnected from all sources and grounded on both sides. Badly eroded parts are replaced.
reference: IEEE C37.30.1-2022, D.4 items b) and d)

question: An outdoor air switch is installed at 2,000 m elevation. Under C37.30.1, this matters because:
choices: Altitude has no effect on air-insulated switches
It is above the 1000 m (3300 ft) usual service limit, so altitude correction factors apply to its ratings
Only the operating handle needs to be changed
The switch must be filled with SF6
explanation: Thinner air cools less and insulates less, so temperature rise goes up and dielectric strength goes down. The usual service conditions stop at 1000 m, and above that the guide applies correction factors to the ratings.
